intro: Creating local networks that reduce food waste while strengthening neighborhood relationships and practical solidarity.

body.heading: Purpose
body.text:
Our food system is broken. Currently, it is the primarly driver for the transgression of our planetary boundaries. In Finland alone, 1.1 tons of edible food is thrown away every single day (Natural Resources Institute Finland). 

**Ultimately, the question is not whether we transition away from the current system but rather how and to where?**

 For the past 3 years, I have worked on food system change from the end of the value chain, focusing on the reduction of food waste through Aalto Foodsharing in Finland. We are an initiative at the intersection of community-led grassroots action, public awareness, and political advocacy. Our goal is to become a global movement in tackling food waste.

body.heading: Operations
body.text:
I am mainly responsible for overseeing, improving and expanding our day-to-day operations, including managing our volunteer network and relationships with food business partners.

This is where my background in service design becomes particularly relevant. I identify challenges and develope practical solutions to adress them. This involves, for example questions of: 

→  How can we improve the onboarding experience for new volunteers? 
→ How can we make the food pick-up process smoother and more efficient for both volunteers and food suppliers?
→ How can we better reach and engage new food business partners through, for example, tailored information materials and introductory packages? 
→ And how can we ensure that our community fridge spaces remain clean, accessible and well-maintained?

body.heading: Outreach & Advocacy
body.text: I also support with organizing and hosting of events for outreach and advocacy purposes. These include, for example, community dinners and cookouts, food system talks, workshop with experts on food conservation, pop-up food distributions or public activism actions. Further we enagage in various networks and with local and national actors, such as the Tipping Point Conference in Helsinki or the Oulu Food Waste Festival, to share our best practices and way of working and to advocate for systemic changes in food policy.
[» Learn more on our website](https://foodsharing.fi/)

intro: Practicing a culture of creativity, experimentation and care in relation with nature.

body.heading: Purpose
body.text:
At Test Site, people from various backgrounds come together around a shared interest in experimenting with creative ideas for practical sustainability.

There are many projects going on simultaneously, ranging from solar panel construction and beekeeping to a regernative textile garden or a tasteLAB field kitchen. All these projects host open workshops and events to invite others to join and participate in this learning process.

body.heading: Contribution
body.text: I am mainly involved in two projects. First, the gardening project, where we grow vegetables, herbs and flowers in a regenerative way and share the harvest with the community. Additionally, I experiment with plants through natural dyeing processes or sun-printing techniques. I have also tested various recipes involving stinging nettles. Second, the outdoor summer cafe, where we repurposed the tasteLAB field kitchen into a volunteer-run cafe. Through this project we explored alternative ways of organizing ourselves, including shared governance and collective decision-making.
[» Learn more on our website](https://www.aalto.fi/en/creative-sustainability/the-test-site)

intro: Translating social and ecological principles into actionable, collective practice across sectors and communities.

body.heading: Purpose
body.text:
Our current economic system is primarily concerned with maximizing profits at all costs. This leads not only to the destruction of our planet but also reinforces social inequality.

In response, more than 50 cities and local governments around the world have implemented the Doughnut Economics Framework into their policies and planning processes as a means to reimagine and work towards an alternative economic model that meets the social needs of people within our environmental limits. **Inspired by these examples, we founded DEFI to bring the principles of Doughnut Economics to Finland and put them into practice in our own context.**

body.heading: Tools & Methods
body.text:
Within DEFI, I am mainly involved in developing participatory research tools and methods that engage people in reflecting on the dimensions of the Doughnut framework. By this, we create spaces for people to learn about Doughnut Economics and alternative ways of understanding our economy, but also gather insights into the social and ecological realities of local communities in Otanieme and Espoo. The aim is to better understand where our local context is falling short in meeting social needs and where we are exceeding ecological boundaries.

Specific tools and methods I have co-developed and facilitated, include for example:
→ A Quick Participatory Doughnut Portrait Mapping Canvas to capture community perspectives
→ A Donut Discovery Workshop with 10+ sustainability organisation around Otaniemie to establish partnerships
→ A Step-Inside-the-Donut Workshop with Aalto University students to reflect on our current state of the economy
→ An Interactive Booklet used in a Walkshop with residents of Espoo to learn about lived experiences on social and ecological issues

body.heading: Outcomes
body.text: Through all these projects, we were able to engage and collaborate with a wide range of stakeholders, including local residents, students, sustainability organisations, and city representatives. Ultimately, by this, we hope to plant the seed for a new economic model in Finland and beyond, and we will continue to work towards this goal.
[» Learn more on our website](https://doughnuteconomics.org/organisations-and-networks/doughnut-economics-finland-initiative-defi)

table.topic: Organizing Planetary Practices, a workshop series and co-learning program with diverse expertise in sustainable ways of being, living and making
table.keywords: Knowledge exchange, Co-learning, Angency, Community practices, Planetary boundaries
table.team:
Paul Grandchamp (Graphic Design)
Eric, Ronja, Joseph, Alice, Gabriella, Edoardo, Chiara, Natasha (Workshop Hosts)

intro: Creating collaborative learning spaces that value lived experience, practical knowledge, and everyday sustainability practices.

body.heading: Purpose
body.text: Everyone has a skill to share. I wanted to create a space where we can learn from each other’s knowledge.

body.heading: Process
body.text:
I published an open call where I invited other people to submit their workshop ideas. The call was open to anyone with a skill or practice that could contribute to sustainable ways of being, living, and making. I selected proposals based on their potential to create a diverse program.
 
 While the workshops itself were hosted by the people who submitted the proposals, I supported them in preparation, material sourcing, planning, marketing and documentation.

body.heading: Outcomes
body.text:
The project resulted in a total of 11 hand-on workshops, focusing on:

→ Repairing electronics

→ Fluid art upcycling

→ Processing nettle into fiber

→ Zine Making for reflecting on the issue of hope labour

→ Pizza making with rescued ingredients

→ Collective reflection on wellbeing

→ Reclaiming agency through anger

 Participants described the experience as inspiring, saying it gave them a greater sense of confidence and agency to engage in activities they had previously considered beyond their reach, such as repairing electronics.

 I was awarded with the Campus Sustainability Champion Award by Aalto University - ACRE for outstanding community impact.
[» Learn more on our website](https://www.aalto.fi/en/sustainability-action-booster/planetary-practices-workshops)

intro: Raising awareness on space sustainability through interdisciplinary and international knowledge exchange.

body.heading: Purpose
body.text:
While we often focus on pollution in our air, water and land, orbital pollution remains an invisible challenge in mainstream discussions. The ongoing race for space innovation and technology has led to an increase in the number of satellites and other objects orbiting Earth, resulting in defunct rocket parts left behind and millions of pieces of space debris.

This debris impacts not only current and future scientific missions but also the space infrastructure that supports our everyday lives, from communication and navigation to weather forecasting and environmental monitoring.

body.heading: Process
body.text:
I participated in a Unite! Hackathon in Graz, Austria, where I met students from the other 7 Unite! Alliance universities. Back then, I was not aware of orbital pollution but inspired to learn more about the issue and explore how we could raise awareness and interdisciplinary dialogue.

Together with students from ULisboa and Université Grenoble Alpes, I developed a project proposal for the Unite! Seed Fund, which was successfully selected for funding.

Following this, I was involved in recruiting and selecting five students from each university with diverse academic backgrounds and a shared interest in the topic. Then, we collaboratively designed the three-day programme, including workshop activities, inviting external experts and arranging travel and practical logistics.

body.heading: Outcomes
body.text:
I co-hosted hosted the programm in person, at Université Grenoble Alpes in France. The programme opened with presentations from the students who shared their ongoing projects and research connected to orbital pollution. This was followed by guest lectures and group discussions, which introduced new perspectives and encouraged critical reflection. Further, hands-on activities allowed participants to engage more directly with the underlying tensions of orbital pollution and potential approaches to making space activities more sustainable.

 Overall, participants described that they not only gained new knowledge and insights into the topic, but also built new connections for future collaborations.

**For me, orrganizing and hosting this programm was a particularly valuable experience on a personal level.** Although I had tutored students before, this experience involved a different level of responsibility. I took on both the role of the organiser as well as mentor by guiding a group of students throughout this international programme, including travelling together to another country.
[» Learn more on our website](https://www.unite-university.eu/unitenews/unite-students-join-forces-for-the-orbiting-sustainability-workshop-in-grenoble)
